metadata.title: PGE and BC Railway identity and corporate milestones
metadata.scope: Sourced railway logo applications and corporate events, supplementing existing establishment, legal-name and ownership records.
metadata.precision_policy: Observation dates are not adoption dates. Approximate years, application-specific transitions and bounded date ranges remain qualified. Concurrent corporate, equipment and passenger-car marks do not form a universal replacement sequence.

events.title: PGE diamond monogram documented on the steam tug Point Ellice

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Greg M. Kennelly, “Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway,” PDF p. 5, paragraph citing Norm Gidney’s dated photograph

events.interpretation_notes: The date belongs to the earliest dated photograph Kennelly identified, not a proven logo introduction. He reports use into the early 1950s. Don Davis is a recollected designer attribution, not a confirmed credit.

events.title: Around 1934: PGE introduces a second, square-diamond logo family

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF pp. 5–6, second diamond-logo paragraphs

events.interpretation_notes: Approximate introduction: the article says around 1934, so no month or day is supplied. Shaded and unshaded versions were used. The unshaded version is illustrated from an undated Ernie Plant photograph of steam crane 6071.

events.title: Shaded PGE square-diamond logo photographed on refrigerator cars

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF p. 6, paragraph citing Charles Bates’s February 1935 photographs

events.interpretation_notes: This dates photographs of refrigerator cars 801–803, not the family’s introduction. The article documents the shaded family on cars 801–806 during at least 1935–1946 and also records related versions on Engineering Combination Coach 16. Recollections that only refrigerator cars used it are qualified by those photographs.

events.title: PGE circular script corporate monogram attested on a company pass

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF p. 6, circular corporate logo paragraph

events.interpretation_notes: 1935 is the earliest application seen by the author, not a verified launch year. The monogram appeared on passes and menus; the author found no evidence of use on rolling stock. Menu versions often used a single narrow border.

events.title: PGE introduces its early caribou equipment herald

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF pp. 6–7, 1945 contest account and first equipment-caribou paragraph

events.interpretation_notes: The article places application to new Mikado locomotives in the second quarter of 1945; year precision is retained rather than inventing a day. Ed Aldridge won the contest with a landscape design; the railway changed the inner scene to a caribou. The published dinner-plate landscape is neither his actual submission nor an adopted logo. Both facing directions and application-specific proportions existed.

events.title: Mid-1946: PGE revises the equipment caribou to a full-profile design

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF p. 8, first paragraph and Mikado 163 illustration

events.interpretation_notes: The source says mid-1946, not an exact month or day. Its illustrated example was traced by the article’s author from a builder photograph of Mikado 163. The mark was applied through the 1950s with differences in neck shading, chest bib and size; it coexisted with separate corporate-printing versions.

events.title: Light-lettered PGE corporate caribou first appears on a public timetable

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF p. 7, paragraph beginning with the 30 September 1946 public timetable

events.interpretation_notes: This dates corporate timetable use, not first use of any caribou emblem: equipment versions already existed. Except for business-car tail signs, the author reports that this corporate artwork was not used on rolling stock.

events.title: PGE introduces Roman-lettered caribou heralds for passenger cars

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF p. 8, Roman-lettered passenger-car paragraph

events.interpretation_notes: The article dates the 24/14-inch variant to 1947. Anderson Lake, Seton Lake and Williams Lake sleepers are believed to have been its first applications. The printed illustration was traced from preserved sleeper Clinton in 1973; 1973 dates that observation, not adoption.

events.title: PGE corporate caribou lettering changes from light to bold during 1948

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF p. 7, public-timetable lettering change bounded by 31 May and 26 September 1948

events.interpretation_notes: The change occurred sometime between the two dates; neither bound is asserted as its exact adoption day. This corporate-printing change does not replace every contemporary equipment or passenger-car variant.

events.title: PGE introduces an oval advertising caribou with the Howe Sound extension

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF p. 8, final paragraph on completion of the Squamish–North Vancouver extension

events.interpretation_notes: The oval corporate mark appeared in newspaper advertisements, brochures and timetables 73C and 73L. By Timetable 75 the 1948 circular corporate mark had returned. The author reports no use of the oval logo on equipment.

events.title: PGE initials replace the caribou on public-timetable front covers

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF p. 7, public-timetable corporate-logo chronology

events.interpretation_notes: This is an application-specific change. Caribou use continued on back covers until 19 January 1966 and on other equipment; it is not a universal withdrawal date.

events.title: BC map mark replaces the caribou on PGE public timetables

evidence.source_title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
evidence.locator: Kennelly, PDF p. 7, final dates in the corporate-caribou paragraph

events.interpretation_notes: The date establishes takeover on public timetables. It does not establish the first appearance of the BC map logo on every railway application. The issue shows only small map-herald examples in the PDF p. 14 livery diagrams.

events.title: British Columbia Railway name enters public use

evidence.source_title: Canadian Rail 248, September 1972
evidence.locator: Canadian Rail 248 (September 1972), printed p. 265 / PDF p. 5, opening name-change paragraph

events.interpretation_notes: Contemporary reporting places the public change on 1 April 1972. The statutory legal-name change is separately recorded on 30 March 1972. This was continuity of the same company, not a merger or newly incorporated Crown.

events.title: New British Columbia Railway dogwood corporate symbol documented

evidence.source_title: Canadian Rail 248, September 1972
evidence.locator: Canadian Rail 248 (September 1972), printed p. 278 / PDF p. 18, new-corporate-symbol caption; PDF p. 19, railway-supplied car photograph

events.interpretation_notes: The contemporary caption identifies the dogwood as the new corporate symbol. Year precision records the documented identity; no precise launch day or universal lettering variant is inferred. The January 1991 Cariboo masthead is a later reproduction, not a 1972 original.

events.title: BC Harbours Board railway assets transfer to British Columbia Railway Company

evidence.source_title: 1985 Report of the Auditor General of British Columbia
evidence.locator: 1985 Report of the Auditor General of British Columbia, PDF pp. 110–111, note 8(c), and PDF p. 166, note 8(b)

events.interpretation_notes: The report dates the asset transfers to 31 October 1983 and distinguishes railway assets transferred to BCR from other assets transferred to BC Development Corporation. This is separate from the Board’s legal dissolution on 30 May 1985. The URL filename says 1984, but the document is the 1985 report reviewing the year ended 31 March 1984.

events.title: BCR transfers railway and property assets to operating and property subsidiaries

evidence.source_title: Environmental Appeal Board decision 2000-WAS-018(b)
evidence.locator: Environmental Appeal Board decision 2000-WAS-018(b), PDF pp. 3–4, “Corporate History of the BCR Group”

events.interpretation_notes: BCR Properties Ltd. was incorporated on 18 May 1984 and S.C. Holdings Ltd. was renamed BC Rail Ltd. on 28 May; asset transfers followed on 12 June. British Columbia Railway Company remained the parent. These legal steps are distinct from the public BC Rail name dated 19 June 1984. The decision’s shorthand Corporation for the 1972 parent is not adopted as its legal name.

events.title: BC Rail name adopted for the railway’s public identity

evidence.source_title: Canadian Rail 547, March–April 2012
evidence.locator: Canadian Rail 547 (March–April 2012), printed p. 49 / PDF p. 5, historical overview

events.interpretation_notes: The museum journal dates the BC Rail name to 19 June 1984. This is a name/identity milestone, not proof of the launch day of a particular red-and-blue graphic, livery or wordmark. It is distinct from the May–June 1984 subsidiary restructuring.

events.title: BCR Partnership created as part of the railway group

evidence.source_title: Environmental Appeal Board decision 2000-WAS-018(b)
evidence.locator: Environmental Appeal Board decision 2000-WAS-018(b), PDF pp. 3–4, “Corporate History of the BCR Group”

events.interpretation_notes: The partnership is distinct from the statutory parent company and the BC Rail Ltd. operating subsidiary. Its units later formed part of the 2004 CN transaction.

events.title: CN transaction closes for the BC Rail operating business

evidence.source_title: BC government: $1-billion investment partnership agreement released
evidence.locator: BC government release of 12 August 2004, agreement descriptions and closing paragraph

events.interpretation_notes: The formal closing transferred BC Rail Ltd. shares and BCR Partnership units to CN. British Columbia Railway Company survived; the transaction provided CN freight-operation rights over publicly owned track and right-of-way. This is not a dissolution or simple renaming of BCRC to CN.

events.title: TSB’s retrospective account dates CN’s acquisition of the BCR system to 15 July 2004

evidence.source_title: Transportation Safety Board railway investigation R05V0141
evidence.locator: Transportation Safety Board report R05V0141, BC Rail/CN acquisition background
evidence.access_note: The acquisition-date passage was available in the official page’s search index on 12 November 2026; direct page retrieval returned HTTP 403.

events.interpretation_notes: An attributed date claim retained for provenance. The TSB describes an acquisition, not a separately established next-day operating transition. Contemporary provincial and CN releases date formal closing to 14 July 2004; CN’s audited statements also date the start of phased integration to 14 July. This record does not establish a distinct 15 July operational milestone or transfer of the Crown parent or publicly owned corridor to CN.

events.title: Audited statements document continuing BCRC railway and port assets

evidence.source_title: BCRC consolidated financial statements, year ended 31 March 2025
evidence.locator: BCRC consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, PDF p. 9, note 1 “Reporting Entity”

events.interpretation_notes: At the reporting date BCRC remains wholly owned by BCTFA, holds the former BC Rail right-of-way and track infrastructure leased to CN, and retains the Port Subdivision operation and BCR Properties activities. This is a dated observation, not a new corporation or an invented 2025 ownership start.
